title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation failure in which AI-generated content was used to fabricate a credible-looking interview between two real, named public figures. The fake article was designed to lend legitimacy to an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform called Boulder Sparhaven. The failure occurred entirely outside any regulated AI deployment, as scammers used generative tools to produce deceptive material rather than any legitimate service malfunctioning.

The point where detection could have intervened was at the publishing or distribution layer, where platforms carrying the fabricated content could in principle have checked whether the interview existed or whether the financial service it promoted held a valid licence. ASIC reported removing tens of thousands of scam pages, which confirms that detection is happening but at scale insufficient to prevent harm before exposure. The mechanism here is straightforward: a model asserting fabricated events as fact, dressed in the appearance of journalism, to redirect victims toward an unlicensed investment scheme.

What is not established is the identity of the scammers, the full extent of financial harm to victims, or whether any platform carrying the content knowingly did so.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler was used to promote Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The fabricated interview never occurred but was designed to appear credible through AI-generated content. This scam represents a growing trend that the Australian Securities and Investments Commission has flagged as increasingly sophisticated and prevalent.

ASIC's recent research shows investment scams jumped significantly, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. The watchdog took down 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, politician Pauline Hanson, billionaire Gina Rinehart, and presenter Alan Kohler are among the most commonly impersonated Australians. ASIC warns consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers and check official registers before investing, though Kohler argues platforms carrying such content should face heavy fines.
